notes: Slot 0 National Party (Vorster), using the NNP sprite as the same organization's successor. Coalition slot 13 holds the Afrikaner Broederbond, the NP's governing power bloc (the NP governed alone). BOSS (founded 1969) in 7. HNP (founded Oct 1969) in 20, which has starting popularity. ANC 5, SACP 4, PAC 18 follow MD with MD sprites. Progressive Party uses the DP/DA sprite as its institutional ancestor; SADF uses the SANDF sprite.

0.name: Nasionale Party
0.text:
The National Party has governed South Africa since 1948 and built the system of apartheid. Prime Minister B. J. Vorster, who succeeded the assassinated Hendrik Verwoerd in 1966, leads it on 1 January 1970, weeks after expelling the arch-conservatives who formed the Herstigte Nasionale Party and ahead of an early general election in April.

The party stands for white supremacy through separate development, the homelands policy and strict security laws against the banned liberation movements. Vorster pursues an outward policy of dialogue with friendly African states while presenting South Africa as an anti-communist bastion for the West. Its base is the Afrikaner electorate, the civil service, the farmers and a growing number of English-speaking whites.

1.name: Verenigde Party
1.text:
The United Party was formed in 1934 by the fusion of Hertzog's and Smuts's parties and governed until 1948. Since then it has been the official opposition, led since 1956 by Sir De Villiers Graaff. It holds a little under a third of the seats in the House of Assembly and draws most of its support from English-speaking whites.

The party offers white leadership with justice, a federal scheme in place of the homelands and a softer racial policy without accepting majority rule. Strongly pro-British and pro-Western, it promises better relations with the Commonwealth. Its strength lies in Natal, the Cape and the business community, but its policy is blurred by a conservative wing that drifts toward the government.

2.name: Progressive Party
2.text:
The Progressive Party was founded in 1959 by liberal members who broke away from the United Party. Led by Jan Steytler, it has only one member of parliament, Helen Suzman of Houghton, who stands alone in the House of Assembly against detention without trial and the pass laws. Since 1968 the law bars it from having black members.

The Progressives demand a qualified non-racial franchise, an entrenched bill of rights and the gradual dismantling of apartheid. They are firmly pro-Western and anti-communist. Their support comes from affluent English-speaking voters in Johannesburg and Cape Town, from academics and from leading businessmen, notably circles close to Harry Oppenheimer, which give them influence far beyond their seats.

3.name: Labour Party
3.text:
The Labour Party was founded in 1965 in the Coloured community and, led by M. D. 'Sonny' Leon, won most elected seats in the first Coloured Persons' Representative Council in 1969. The government nevertheless filled the nominated seats with its own supporters and handed control of the council to the rival Federal Party.

The party rejects apartheid and uses the council as a platform to demand full citizenship and a common voters' roll. It stands for social democracy, trade-union rights, housing and education for working people. Its base lies in the Western Cape and among Coloured teachers and workers, and its leverage comes from exposing the separate institutions as hollow.

4.name: South African Communist Party
4.text:
The South African Communist Party was founded in 1921, banned in 1950 and reconstituted underground in 1953. Its chairman J. B. Marks and general secretary Moses Kotane work from exile in Tanzania and Moscow, while leaders such as Bram Fischer serve life sentences. Joe Slovo and other cadres help direct the armed struggle.

The party seeks a national democratic revolution leading to socialism and is one of Moscow's most loyal allies in Africa. Its alliance with the ANC gives it great influence inside Umkhonto we Sizwe and in channelling Soviet bloc arms and training. Inside the country its networks are almost destroyed, but its exile apparatus remains disciplined and well-funded.

5.name: African National Congress
5.text:
The African National Congress, founded in 1912, was banned in 1960 after Sharpeville and turned to armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe. Nelson Mandela, Walter Sisulu and others serve life sentences on Robben Island, and Oliver Tambo leads the movement in exile. At Morogoro in 1969 it opened its external membership to all races and adopted a new strategy.

The ANC upholds the Freedom Charter's vision of a non-racial democracy and works in alliance with the SACP. It relies on Soviet and Eastern bloc support, bases in Tanzania and Zambia, and recognition across Africa. Underground at home, its strength lies in the loyalty of millions and its standing as the leading voice of the oppressed.

6.name: Nederduitse Gereformeerde Kerk
6.text:
The Dutch Reformed Church is the largest Afrikaans church and a pillar of Afrikaner society, with separate mission churches for black, Coloured and Indian members. After the Cottesloe consultation of 1960 it left the World Council of Churches, and its leadership remains close to the National Party.

The church provides theological justification for separate development and condemns the liberal theology of the Western ecumenical movement as a threat to the Afrikaner volk. It resists secular modernity, permissive culture and international pressure alike. Its leverage lies in the pulpit and in the dominees who shape opinion in every town, though critics such as Beyers Naudé have challenged it from within.
6.wiki: Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa (NGK)

7.name: Buro vir Staatsveiligheid
7.text:
The Bureau for State Security was created in 1969 under General Hendrik van den Bergh, Vorster's closest confidant since their internment together during the Second World War. It absorbs the security police's intelligence functions and reports directly to the Prime Minister.

BOSS hunts the ANC, PAC and SACP at home and abroad, spies on liberal opponents and conducts secret diplomacy with African states. Its sweeping powers and secrecy make it feared even inside the National Party, and it treats Western criticism as hostile action. Its leverage rests on van den Bergh's personal access to Vorster and on files that can ruin careers.

8.name: Ahl al-Bayt Jamaat
8.text:
The Ahl al-Bayt Jamaat is a small community of Shia Muslims among the Indian families of Durban and Johannesburg, many of Khoja origin with ties to East Africa. It maintains a modest prayer hall and organises religious classes and Muharram gatherings.

The community values education, commerce and peaceful coexistence and keeps out of party politics. Classified as Indian under apartheid, its members suffer the Group Areas Act and resent forced removals from their trading districts. Its influence is limited to its own members, but its trading and family networks across the Indian Ocean link it to the wider Shia world.

9.name: Karbala Youth
9.text:
Karbala Youth is a devotional circle of young Shia men in Durban who gather around preachers trained in Najaf and Qom. Its members study clerical writings and organise the processions of Muharram.

They insist on obedience to the senior Shia clergy and see both apartheid and Western secular culture as manifestations of injustice. They have no political organisation and only a handful of followers, but they absorb the ideas of activist clerics in Iraq and Iran and could become a channel for revolutionary Shia thought should the wider Shia world turn militant.

10.name: Muslim Judicial Council
10.text:
The Muslim Judicial Council was founded in Cape Town in 1945 as the body of imams and scholars serving the Cape Muslim community. It rules on religious law, supervises halal certification and speaks for the mosques of the Cape Peninsula.

The council is cautious and conservative, concentrating on religious life and avoiding confrontation with the state. It condemns forced removals under the Group Areas Act, which threaten mosques in District Six and elsewhere, but prefers petitions to protest. After the death in detention of Imam Abdullah Haron in 1969 younger Muslims press it to speak out, and its leverage lies in its authority over the Cape mosques.

11.name: Muhajirun Circle
11.text:
The Muhajirun Circle is a tiny group of young Muslims in Cape Town and Johannesburg who studied in Pakistan, Egypt or Saudi Arabia and returned with literature on the caliphate. Embittered by the death of Imam Abdullah Haron in police custody, they see apartheid as proof that Muslims cannot live under unbelievers.

The circle rejects both the white state and the secular liberation movements and dreams of a united Islamic order. It condemns the West and the Soviet Union alike. It has no arms and few members, meets in private homes and survives only because the security police consider it insignificant.

12.name: Claremont Muslim Youth Association
12.text:
The Claremont Muslim Youth Association was founded in Cape Town in 1958 around Imam Abdullah Haron of the Stegman Road mosque. Haron used it and the Muslim News to preach social justice, until he was detained under the Terrorism Act and died in police custody in September 1969. His funeral drew tens of thousands.

The association combines Islamic education with social engagement and condemns apartheid as un-Islamic. It works with Christian and secular opponents of the regime and inspires a generation of politically conscious Muslims. Its influence lies among students, teachers and young professionals of the Cape, and Haron's martyrdom gives it moral weight far beyond its numbers.

13.name: Afrikaner Broederbond
13.text:
The Afrikaner Broederbond is a secret society founded in 1918 whose members hold key positions throughout the state, the churches, the universities and the Afrikaans press. Chaired by Piet Meyer, also head of the South African Broadcasting Corporation, it counts almost every National Party cabinet minister among its members.

The Bond works to secure Afrikaner power and Christian-national values through patronage, appointments and policy planning behind closed doors. It guards apartheid's ideological purity while trying to hold the National Party together after the split with the HNP. Its leverage lies in its unseen control of appointments and its ability to settle disputes before they reach the public.

14.name: Transkei National Independence Party
14.text:
The Transkei National Independence Party governs the Transkei, the first homeland to receive self-government in 1963. It is led by Chief Kaiser Matanzima, chief minister since 1963, who relies on the nominated chiefs in the legislative assembly to keep a majority over Knowledge Guzana's opposition.

The party accepts separate development as a route to self-rule for the Xhosa and campaigns for more land, Xhosa-language schooling and the transfer of white-owned towns. It is authoritarian, deeply rooted in the chieftaincy and neither Western nor Eastern in outlook. Its leverage lies in Pretoria's need for a showcase homeland and in Matanzima's control of patronage in Umtata.

15.name: Anglo American Corporation
15.text:
The Anglo American Corporation of South Africa, founded in 1917 by Ernest Oppenheimer, dominates gold, diamonds through De Beers, coal, industry and finance. Its chairman Harry Oppenheimer, a former United Party MP, is the richest and most powerful businessman on the continent.

Anglo American regards apartheid's job reservation and migrant-labour system as obstacles to growth and quietly funds liberal causes and the Progressive Party. It remains firmly Western-oriented and depends on stable relations with London and New York. Its leverage lies in mines, capital and foreign investment, which no government in Pretoria can ignore, though Afrikaner nationalists despise its wealth and influence.

16.name: Afrikaanse Handelsinstituut
16.text:
The Afrikaanse Handelsinstituut was founded in 1942 to advance Afrikaner businessmen in commerce, industry and finance, then dominated by English-speaking capital. By 1970 it represents a confident new class of Afrikaner entrepreneurs, from Sanlam and Rembrandt to small-town traders.

The institute calls for free enterprise, lower taxes and fewer controls, and increasingly argues that rigid labour laws and job reservation hinder growth. It supports the National Party but pushes its leaders toward pragmatic, market-friendly policies. Its leverage lies in its access to ministers through Afrikaner networks and in the growing economic weight of its members.

17.name: Wildlife Protection and Conservation Society of South Africa
17.english: Wildlife Protection and Conservation Society of South Africa
17.text:
The Wildlife Protection and Conservation Society of South Africa grew out of the Wild Life Protection Society founded in 1926. It campaigns for nature reserves, endangered species and environmental education, and helped build public support for the Kruger National Park and provincial reserves.

The society argues for protecting wilderness, curbing pollution and soil erosion, and planning water use in a dry country. It avoids party politics and draws its members mainly from the English-speaking middle class, hunters-turned-conservationists and scientists. Its leverage lies in public education, lobbying of provincial administrations and the prestige of South Africa's parks abroad.
17.wiki: Wildlife and Environment Society of South Africa

18.name: Pan Africanist Congress
18.text:
The Pan Africanist Congress broke away from the ANC in 1959 under Robert Sobukwe and led the anti-pass campaign that ended in the Sharpeville massacre. Banned in 1960, it saw its armed wing Poqo crushed. Sobukwe was released from Robben Island in 1969 but is banished to Kimberley, while Potlako Leballo leads the exile movement from Tanzania.

The PAC calls for Africa for the Africans, rejects the ANC's alliance with white communists and stands for an Africanist socialism. It seeks support from China and from African states rather than Moscow. Its exiled leadership is torn by factional strife, but its appeal survives among township youth and students.

19.name: Non-European Unity Movement
19.text:
The Non-European Unity Movement was founded in 1943 by Coloured and African intellectuals in the Western Cape. Its leading figure, I. B. Tabata, works from exile in Zambia, and its African People's Democratic Union of Southern Africa organises in the Transkei and among teachers in the Cape.

The movement preaches non-collaboration with all apartheid institutions and the boycott of dummy councils. It advocates a democratic and socialist South Africa and rejects both Moscow's line and the ANC's alliance politics, drawing on independent Marxist and Trotskyist ideas. Its influence lies among teachers, students and intellectuals, where its rigorous principles shape a generation even as its organisation is harassed.

20.name: Herstigte Nasionale Party
20.text:
The Herstigte Nasionale Party was founded in October 1969 by Albert Hertzog and Jaap Marais after their expulsion from the National Party. They accuse Vorster of betraying Verwoerd's legacy through sports contacts with mixed teams, diplomatic ties with black African states and courting English-speaking voters.

The HNP stands for uncompromising apartheid, Calvinist Christian nationalism and Afrikaans as the sole national language. It denounces Anglo-American capitalism and Western liberalism as threats to the volk. Its base is among conservative farmers, workers and clergymen in the Transvaal, and its leverage lies in pressure on the National Party's right flank rather than in seats.

21.name: Die Stormjaers
21.text:
Die Stormjaers takes its name from the paramilitary wing of the wartime Ossewabrandwag, the pro-German Afrikaner movement that dissolved in 1952. Its members are aging veterans of the old Ossewabrandwag and younger admirers who gather in shooting clubs, cultural societies and far-right reading circles.

They dream of a Boer republic based on authoritarian leadership, racial purity and the destruction of communism, and despise parliamentary democracy and international finance. They feel betrayed by former comrades who now hold office and are drawn to the HNP. Their leverage lies in arms and fervour rather than numbers.

22.name: Suid-Afrikaanse Weermag
22.text:
The South African Defence Force, the strongest military in sub-Saharan Africa, is commanded by General Rudolph Hiemstra under Defence Minister P. W. Botha. Conscription of white men has expanded steadily since 1967, and the force increasingly builds its own arms industry through Armscor in defiance of the UN arms embargo.

The SADF prepares for a total onslaught by communist-backed insurgents, supports Rhodesia and Portugal and operates against SWAPO in South West Africa. Its officers are loyal to the government and see South Africa as a Western bastion. Its leverage is growing as Botha champions the armed forces and military thinking within the cabinet.

23.name: Zulu Royal House
23.text:
The Zulu Royal House descends from Shaka and Cetshwayo, kings of the Zulu nation. After the death of King Cyprian Bhekuzulu in 1968, Prince Goodwill Zwelithini was named heir, while Prince Israel Mcwayizeni acts as regent. Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi serves as the royal family's traditional adviser.

Royalists seek recognition of the king as the symbol of Zulu unity and resist Pretoria's attempts to turn the monarchy into a tool of the homeland system. They want land, dignity and authority for the Zulu nation. Their leverage lies in the loyalty of millions of Zulu-speakers in Natal and the reef hostels.
